newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Britain's Major heads back to political battles.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Major heads back to political battles.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major rushed back from Pakistan on Tuesday after a week-long South Asian tour for a crucial parliamentary vote.
Major has been feted and praised on his tour of India, Pakistan and Bangladesh, where he has been trying to boost British trade.
But Tuesday's dash showed that the realities of British politics, with a general election now less than four months away, are firmly back at the top of the agenda.
Major, who has refused to detail the actual election date, said that despite the prospect of open parliamentary warfare from now on, he was prepared to hang on in power as long as possible.
"I am prepared to play it long, of course I am prepared to play it long," he told British journalists before flying out of Lahore an hour earlier than scheduled.
But he said that the Conservative party was "ready for the election whenever it comes".
Major faces an uphill battle to win the election and secure the Conservative government's fifth term in office.

After 17 years of Conservative rule, many voters have been put off by the Conservatives following a string of sleaze scandals and are attracted to the opposition Labour Party by its move to the centre under new party leader Tony Blair.
Opinion polls put Major some 20 points behind Labour.

But the British prime minister said he believed voters would start swinging back to the Conservatives when they realised what was at stake. "When people begin to focus on the policy of the two parties, that is when they will ask the serious questions.
"They will say, 'Are things going right now and would they change if we change government?'," said a defiant Major.
Accusing Labour of having no policies, he said voting for them would be a "leap in the dark".
And in a bitter attack on his rivals, he said: "The opposition have been in opposition for 18 years. They are very good at it. They are so good at it that they should stay in opposition."
Major said his government had had to take difficult economic decisions but their fruits -- soaring growth, falling unemployment, and low inflation and interest rates -- were now beginning to be felt.
"It is a great advantage to go into the election with the best economy in Western Europe," he declared.
But despite his confidence, the decision to fly back an hour earlier shows the difficulties he will face to hang onto power in the coming months.

In protest at what it described as cheating in a vote before Christmas, a charge hotly disputed by Major, the opposition has ditched usual parliamentary courtesies which allow members of parliament to be absent if previously agreed with a member of the opposite side.
This means the government will have to insist that its MPs turn up for every important vote and it risks an ambush at any moment.
Major no longer has an overall majority in parliament, although he can usually rely on MPs from Northern Irish Unionist parties.
The vote on Tuesday night is on the finance bill, which puts the budget into effect.
